report.tagline: A UK bank that lives only in an app, for people and small businesses, which also sells its banking software to other banks.
report.simpleSummary: Starling is a proper UK bank, but with no branches. You open a current account on your phone in minutes, and the app shows every payment instantly, splits bills and sorts your spending. It is especially popular with small businesses and sole traders. It also sells the software it built to run itself, called Engine, to banks in other countries.

overview.whatItDoes: Starling offers free personal, joint and business current accounts in an app, plus savings, loans and overdrafts. It earns most of its money by lending out deposits and earning interest. Its software arm, Engine, rents the same technology to other banks, such as Salt Bank in Romania and AMP Bank in Australia.
howItWorks: You download the app, scan your ID and take a video selfie. The account is open in minutes, with a card on its way and a digital card ready for Apple Pay or Google Pay.
Every payment shows up in real time with the shop name and category, so you always know your balance.
Spaces let you set aside money for bills or goals, and Bills Manager pays bills from a separate pot.
Business owners get invoicing, tax estimates, receipt capture and accounting links, with paid add-ons like the Business Toolkit.
Deposits are protected up to £85,000 by the UK government scheme (FSCS), because Starling holds a full banking licence.
Engine packages Starling's own banking system as cloud software for other banks, who pay a setup fee and ongoing licence fees.
overview.valueProposition: A real bank account with no monthly fee, instant notifications and useful tools, without ever visiting a branch. For small businesses, an account that opens in a day instead of weeks.

painPoints.pain: Opening a business account at a high street bank takes weeks.
painPoints.howSolved: App sign-up with checks done digitally, often open the same day.

painPoints.pain: Not knowing your real balance until payments clear.
painPoints.howSolved: Real-time notifications and a live balance on every payment.

painPoints.pain: Fees for using your card abroad.
painPoints.howSolved: No Starling fees on card spending or cash abroad, using the Mastercard rate.

painPoints.pain: Budgeting is hard when everything sits in one balance.
painPoints.howSolved: Spaces, saving goals and Bills Manager separate money by purpose.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Free accounts with instant notifications, card controls and fee-free spending abroad.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Brings in cheap deposits, which Starling lends out at higher rates.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Free business accounts for sole traders and limited companies, with invoicing and multi-user access.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Business deposits are large and sticky, and businesses are its strongest segment.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Pots for goals and bills, with round-ups into a space.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Encourages users to keep more money in Starling and use it as their main account.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Paid add-ons for invoicing, VAT and tax, plus Ember accounting software it bought in 2024.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Adds subscription revenue that does not depend on interest rates.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Overdrafts, personal loans, mortgages through its Fleet arm and business loans.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Lending is where it earns interest; growing it safely is the main profit lever.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Starling's banking software sold to banks abroad as a cloud service.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: A second business with software-like margins, less tied to UK interest rates.

steps.detail: Finds Starling through an accountant or comparison site and installs the app.
Picks sole trader or limited company. For a company, Starling checks Companies House.
Scans passport or driving licence and records a short selfie video.
Gets sort code and account number, often the same day, and a digital card.
Creates an invoice in the app and shares a link.
Pays monthly for the Business Toolkit to handle VAT and tax returns.
Signs up in the app in about 10 minutes.
Moves salary, direct debits and balance from the old bank in 7 working days.
Creates spaces for rent, holidays and an emergency fund.
Card payments round up to the nearest pound into a saving space.
Spends on holiday with no Starling fee and gets instant alerts.
Applies in the app with a decision shown on screen.
Looks at Salt Bank in Romania, which launched on Engine and signed up customers fast.
Engine team agrees which products to launch and which local systems to connect.
Bank pays an upfront setup fee and agrees yearly licence fees.
Engine configures the platform and connects to local payment systems.
Bank launches its app to customers on Engine's cloud platform.
Fees grow as the bank adds customers and products.

businessModel.summary: Starling makes most of its money as a lender: it pays little or no interest on current account money and earns more by lending it out or holding it at the Bank of England. It adds card fees, paid business tools and software licence fees from Engine.

revenueStreams.detail: Interest earned on loans and money held at the Bank of England, minus interest paid to savers. The largest share of revenue, so falling rates hurt.
Interchange, a small fee the shop's bank pays each time a Starling card is used.
Monthly fees for the Business Toolkit, Ember accounting and other add-ons.
Setup and licence fees from banks abroad. Small today but growing fast, and less tied to interest rates.

businessModel.pricing: Personal and business current accounts are free with no monthly fee. Business Toolkit is a paid add-on at about £7 a month. Overdrafts and loans have published interest rates based on your credit. Engine pricing is not public.
costDrivers: Staff costs for engineers, support and compliance teams
Fraud and financial crime controls, which the FCA said were too weak during fast growth
Credit losses on loans that are not paid back, including government-backed Covid loans
businessModel.unitEconomics: Take a personal customer who keeps an average of £2,000 in their account. If Starling earns about 4% on that money and pays almost nothing on current account balances, that customer is worth about £80 a year in interest, plus perhaps £20 to £40 a year in card fees. Serving them in an app costs much less than a branch bank, perhaps £30 to £50 a year including support and fraud checks. Business customers hold more money and pay for add-ons, so they are worth more. When interest rates fall, the £80 shrinks fast, which is why Starling is pushing Engine and paid tools.

howTheyGetUsers: Word of mouth and strong app store ratings
Accountants and business networks recommending it to sole traders
Current Account Switch Service from other banks
Comparison sites and 'best business bank' awards
Engine sales to banks abroad through direct enterprise selling
whatBringsUsersBack: Salary paid in, so it becomes the main daily account
Spaces and Bills Manager that run the month's money
Business tools like invoicing and tax used weekly
growth.moat: Starling built its own core banking system in-house instead of renting one, and it holds a full UK banking licence. That combination lets it launch features fast and run cheaply, and it can sell the same system to other banks. A new rival would need years and a licence to copy it.

competitors.name: Monzo
competitors.positioning: The biggest UK app bank, popular with young people, with paid plans.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Starling has fewer customers but is older in business banking and was profitable earlier. Monzo leans on subscriptions and a younger brand.

competitors.name: Revolut
competitors.positioning: Global money app with trading, crypto and travel, now a UK bank.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Starling is UK-focused and simpler, with a stronger position with small businesses.

competitors.name: Tide
competitors.positioning: App-based business account for small firms.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Tide is not a full bank in the UK, so Starling can offer FSCS protection and its own lending.

competitors.name: High street banks (Barclays, Lloyds, NatWest)
competitors.positioning: Branches, mortgages and a full range of products.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Starling is faster to open, cheaper to run and has a better-rated app, but a smaller product range.

competitors.name: Thought Machine and Mambu
competitors.positioning: Core banking software sold to banks.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Engine's pitch is that it runs a real profitable bank, while these sell software only.

northStar.metric: Number of customers who use Starling as their main account (salary or business takings paid in each month)
northStar.why: A main account means the customer trusts Starling with their money and uses it daily. That brings deposits and card spend, which drive revenue. Raw sign-ups do not show this, since many people open an app account and never use it. That is what makes it a good north star metric: it moves only when customers get real value.

strengths: Profitable for five years in a row, unlike many app banks
Own technology means fast changes and low running costs
Strong reputation with sole traders and small businesses
Engine gives it a second, global business
Full UK banking licence with FSCS deposit protection
weaknesses: Profit depends heavily on interest rates, which have been falling
The 2024 FCA fine showed weak financial crime controls, and it was told to limit high-risk customers for a time
Losses on government-backed Covid loans (Bounce Back Loans) created provisions

pmLessons: Building your own core technology is expensive at first but can become a product you sell.
Growth without strong controls can cost you: the FCA fine slowed Starling down. Safety features are product features.
A bank's profit depends on interest rates. A good PM looks for revenue that does not move with the Bank of England.
Picking a segment you can serve best, here small businesses, is a strong way to compete with bigger rivals.

interviewQuestions.question: Interest rates are falling. How would you grow Starling's revenue?
interviewQuestions.hint: Split revenue by stream. Look at fee income (Toolkit, Ember), lending growth with controlled risk, and Engine. Prioritise by size and speed. Name a guardrail like credit losses.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Starling launch in another country or focus on Engine?
interviewQuestions.hint: Compare cost, licence time, competition and capital needs. Engine lets it go global without a licence in each country. Pick one and explain the trade-off.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you increase the number of customers who use Starling as their main account?
interviewQuestions.hint: Define main account. Find why people keep salary elsewhere. Ideas: switch rewards, salary advance, better budgeting. Metric: salary paid-in share.

interviewQuestions.question: Design an experience for a customer whose account is frozen for checks.
interviewQuestions.hint: Balance user empathy with compliance. Show status, what is needed and a timeline, without tipping off criminals. Metric: time to resolve, complaints.

interviewQuestions.question: What metrics would you track for Engine?
interviewQuestions.hint: Contracts signed, time to launch, end customers on client banks, revenue per client, client churn. Explain which is the leading indicator.
